title.en: The Last Light on the Sentiero Azzurro

body.title: The Last Light on the Sentiero Azzurro
body.subtitle: When the day-trippers have gone and the trail belongs to evening

body.quote: There's a particular quality to the light here between six and seven in the evening—honey-thick and slanting, the kind that makes ordinary stone walls look like they're holding secrets.
body.leftContent:
Most people walk the Sentiero Azzurro in the morning. They're up early, beating the heat and the crowds, which makes sense if you're trying to cover all five villages in a day. But they miss this—the hour when the trail exhales, when the limestone path still holds the day's warmth under your feet and the sea below turns from tourist-brochure blue to something deeper, more private.

I'm not saying you should skip the morning walk. The light is beautiful then too, crisp and clear, good for photographs. But if you want to understand why people have been walking this coastline for centuries, why the muleteers and the farmers and the smugglers all took this same route, you need to see it at the end of the day.
body.rightContent:
The climb out of Vernazza is the hardest part—always has been. Three hundred steps, though I've never counted them myself. You can still see the original stone steps laid centuries ago, worn smooth in the middle where generations of feet found the same comfortable groove. The tourists who started at dawn are long gone. The shops are closing. Someone is watering the lemon trees in their terraced garden below, and the smell of it rises up with the basil and the salt.

Your legs complain. Let them. By the time you reach the first real viewpoint—you'll know it when you see it—your breathing has found its rhythm and the village has dropped away behind you.

body.markdown: This is where the trail really begins, where it stops being about getting from one village to another and becomes about the walking itself. The path narrows, pressed between the hillside and the drop to the sea. On your left, the terraces climb up in their ancient geometry—the muretti a secco, dry stone walls that have held these slopes in place for eight hundred years. Someone is still farming up there. You can see the stakes for the vines, the silver-green leaves of olive trees that were old when your grandparents were born.

The light is changing now, getting richer. It catches in the wild fennel growing between the stones, turns the agave flowers into torches. Below, the water is doing that thing it does in the evening, layering itself into bands of color—pale aquamarine close to shore where you can see the rocks, then green, then blue, then that deep almost-purple that means depth, real depth, the kind where the bottom drops away to nothing.

body.alt: Sunlight streaming through olive branches overlooking the Ligurian coast
body.caption: The olive groves along the trail have been here for generations, their roots holding the terraced slopes. Photo by Fredo Gerdes on Unsplash

body.markdown: There's a hidden bay below the path, just past the halfway point to Corniglia. You won't find it on any map worth mentioning, and I'm not going to tell you exactly where it is—some things you find yourself or you don't find at all. But you'll hear it first, the particular sound of water moving over smooth stones, different from the open-sea sound you've been hearing. If you look carefully through the scrub oak and the mastic, you might catch the white flash of surf on rocks, a small crescent of beach that no one has touched since this morning, maybe longer.

My nonna used to say that walking this path in the evening meant you could smell what everyone was making for dinner—the garlic hitting hot olive oil in a hundred different kitchens, the particular sharpness of anchovies being rinsed of their salt, the green smell of basil being torn by hand. The wind carries it up from the villages on both sides. On Thursdays you might catch the wood smoke from the bakery ovens being fired up for tomorrow's focaccia. In October, someone is always making passata, and the whole coast smells like tomatoes being put up for winter.

The train passes below, the evening run heading toward La Spezia. You hear the horn first, then see the silver flash moving between the tunnels. The sound echoes up the rock face, changes pitch in the distance. When I was small, I used to time my walks to the trains, using them the way other people use a watch. The 18:42 meant you had half an hour of good light left. The 19:17 meant you'd better know the path well, because the shadows were getting serious.

body.quote: I walked this section last Tuesday evening, just as the light was starting to go amber. A couple from Milano had the same idea—we passed each other twice, going slow, not talking much. At the Corniglia end, where the path spills out into the village, we nodded at each other, the way you do when you've shared something without having to explain it. They got it. That hour belongs to people who understand that getting there isn't really the point.
body.author: Giulia Rossi

body.markdown: The last section into Corniglia is different. The path widens, becomes more of a proper trail. You're higher now, and the views open up—you can see back to Vernazza, forward to Manarola, the whole sweep of coast laid out like a promise. The light is horizontal now, that last-gasp golden that photographers wait hours for. It makes everything look like it's been dipped in honey—the stone, the vegetation, even your own hands when you look at them.

By the time you reach the village, the light is starting to fail. The street lamps are coming on. Someone is setting tables at the restaurant in the piazza, and the church bells ring for evening Mass, the way they have for five hundred years. You're tired—the good kind of tired, the kind that comes from using your body the way it was meant to be used. Your legs will remember this tomorrow, especially those first steps out of Vernazza.

But for now, find a seat at one of the small bars in the upper village. Order something cold. Watch the sky do its final performance over the water—rose, then orange, then that particular violet that means the day is finished. The trail is dark now. The people who walked it this morning are already at dinner, posting their photos, planning tomorrow's itinerary. They saw the Sentiero Azzurro in daylight, which is fine, which is good. But you saw it in the last light. And that makes all the difference.

body.title: Walking at Golden Hour
body.content:
The evening walk requires some preparation. Bring a headlamp—the last section will be in twilight, and the path, while well-maintained, has some uneven spots. The trail officially closes at sunset, but locals have walked it at dusk for generations. Use your judgment and your common sense.

Start from Vernazza between 5:30 and 6:00 PM in summer, earlier in spring and fall. The walk to Corniglia takes about 90 minutes at an evening pace—slower than your morning speed, and that's the point. You're not racing daylight; you're watching it change.

Water, yes. Snacks, maybe. But leave the photography ambitions for another time. This walk is about being present, about noticing how the color of the water changes minute by minute, about hearing the train and the dinner sounds and your own breathing. The images you take home from this one will be in your head, which is where the best ones belong anyway.
